blocks.content: This topic pulls together nearly everything covered across this entire course into one single, complete story: tracing one real request, from the moment a URL is typed, through every single piece of infrastructure covered in this course, all the way to a response finally rendering on screen.

If any individual step feels unfamiliar, that is exactly the signal to revisit its own full, dedicated topic elsewhere in this course, this topic is deliberately a connecting thread, not a replacement for that depth.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784019119518-495325975.png
blocks.alt: The complete journey: DNS, TCP, TLS, possibly a CDN edge, a load balancer, a gateway or proxy, and finally the backend service

blocks.content: 1. Step One: DNS Resolution

The very first thing that happens, before anything else at all, is a DNS lookup, covered in complete depth in the entire DNS module, translating the typed domain name into an actual, usable IP address. Nothing else in this journey can happen until this step genuinely completes.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784019121761-133056558.png
blocks.alt: The journey always begins with a full DNS resolution, translating the typed domain name into an actual IP address

blocks.content: 2. Step Two: TCP and TLS Handshakes
blocks.text: 2. Step Two: TCP and TLS Handshakes

blocks.content: With an IP address now known, a TCP handshake establishes a reliable connection, covered in full in the TCP Deep Dive module. If the connection is HTTPS, a TLS handshake follows immediately after, covered in full in the ssl-tls-handshake topic, establishing genuine encryption before any real data actually flows.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784019123316-130070268.png
blocks.alt: A TCP handshake establishes reliable connectivity; a TLS handshake, for HTTPS, establishes encryption right after it

blocks.content: 3. Step Three: A Possible CDN Shortcut
blocks.text: 3. Step Three: A Possible CDN Shortcut

blocks.content: For cacheable content, tying directly back to the cdn topic, the request might actually be served directly from a nearby edge server at this point, never needing to travel all the way to the origin infrastructure at all. This is precisely why a CDN can make a request journey dramatically shorter for exactly this kind of content.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784019125405-151046294.png
blocks.alt: For cacheable content, a nearby CDN edge might serve the request directly, ending the journey right there without reaching the origin

blocks.title: Not every request gets this shortcut
blocks.content: Highly personalized or genuinely dynamic content, tying back to the cdn topic own honest limitation, generally cannot take this shortcut, and continues on toward the real origin infrastructure instead.
4. Step Four: The Load Balancer

If the request genuinely does reach the origin infrastructure, it typically first hits a load balancer, covered in full in the load-balancer-networking topic, which distributes it to one of potentially many available backend servers, rather than every single request hitting one single server directly.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784019127067-795513606.png
blocks.alt: At the origin, a load balancer distributes the incoming request to one of potentially many available backend servers

blocks.content: 5. Step Five: A Reverse Proxy or API Gateway
blocks.text: 5. Step Five: A Reverse Proxy or API Gateway

blocks.content: The request may then pass through a reverse proxy or an API gateway, covered in full in their own dedicated topics earlier in this module, which might handle TLS termination, apply authentication or rate limiting, and route the request to the exact correct specific backend service that actually needs to handle it.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784019128671-493678281.png
blocks.alt: A reverse proxy or API gateway may handle TLS, authentication, and routing before finally reaching the correct backend service

blocks.content: {"headers":["Infrastructure piece","What it might do at this stage"],"rows":[["Reverse proxy","TLS termination, caching, hiding real backend servers"],["API gateway","Authentication, rate limiting, routing to the correct service"]]}
6. Step Six: The Actual Backend Service Does Real Work
blocks.text: 6. Step Six: The Actual Backend Service Does Real Work

blocks.content: Finally, the request arrives at the actual backend service responsible for handling it, which does the real, specific work the request actually needs, querying data, running application logic, whatever is genuinely required, and builds an appropriate response.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784019130677-648289092.png
blocks.alt: The actual backend service finally does the real, specific work the request needs, and builds an appropriate response

blocks.title: This is the one truly unique step in the whole journey
blocks.content: Every other step in this journey is genuinely generic infrastructure shared across countless different requests to countless different applications. This one step, the actual backend work, is the only part genuinely specific to what a particular application actually does.
7. Step Seven: The Journey Back

The response then travels back through essentially the same chain of infrastructure it came through, back through any gateway or proxy, back across the established TCP or TLS connection, until it finally arrives back at the original browser, which parses and renders it, exactly the final step covered in the request-response-lifecycle topic.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784019132241-356265724.png
blocks.alt: The response travels back through the same infrastructure chain, finally arriving at the browser to be parsed and rendered

blocks.content: 8. The Full Journey, One Final Time
blocks.text: 8. The Full Journey, One Final Time

blocks.content: Putting every single step together in order tells the complete story: DNS, TCP, TLS, a possible CDN shortcut, a load balancer, a gateway or proxy, the actual backend service doing real work, and finally the response traveling all the way back. Every single piece of this course, from the very first topic to this final module, has a real, concrete place in this one journey.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784019133882-481084528.png
blocks.alt: The complete, full journey of one request, tying together nearly every major topic covered across this entire course

9. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

["Assuming a request travels through a fixed, identical path every single time, when a CDN shortcut can genuinely skip much of this journey entirely for cacheable content.","Treating each piece of infrastructure in this journey as unrelated, when they form one single, coherent, connected system working together.","A request journey genuinely begins with DNS resolution and a TCP or TLS handshake before any application logic runs at all.","A CDN can serve cacheable content directly from the edge, entirely bypassing the origin infrastructure.","Load balancers, reverse proxies, and API gateways each play a genuine, specific role in getting a request to the correct backend service."]
items: Assuming a request travels through a fixed, identical path every single time, when a CDN shortcut can genuinely skip much of this journey entirely for cacheable content.
Treating each piece of infrastructure in this journey as unrelated, when they form one single, coherent, connected system working together.
A request journey genuinely begins with DNS resolution and a TCP or TLS handshake before any application logic runs at all.
A CDN can serve cacheable content directly from the edge, entirely bypassing the origin infrastructure.
Load balancers, reverse proxies, and API gateways each play a genuine, specific role in getting a request to the correct backend service.
